content: The Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) was established by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in 1991 to regulate the levels of lead and copper in public drinking water at the consumer's tap. This rule also aimed to minimize the corrosion of pipes caused by the water itself. The LCR was implemented in response to studies that demonstrated the harmful effects of lead and copper on human health. To achieve its goals, the LCR required improvements in water treatment processes, monitoring of lead and copper levels in households with lead plumbing components, and the elimination of water sources as contributors to lead and copper contamination. If lead and copper levels exceeded the established action levels, water suppliers were mandated to educate consumers on reducing their exposure to lead. A study conducted by the EPA in 2004-2005 found that the LCR was effective in 96% of water systems serving populations of at least 3,300 people. In 1993, an article in the Journal of Environmental Health highlighted that approximately four million lead service line pipes were in use at the time. Lead was historically favored as a material for piping due to its low corrosion rate, which was attributed to the formation of a protective lead carbonate layer on the pipe's surface. However, water with low pH and low calcium levels hindered the formation of calcium carbonate, and the acidity of such water could dissolve lead from the pipes into the water supply. Following the adoption of the LCR in May 1991, water suppliers serving more than 50,000 people were required to evaluate their corrosion control systems and replace their pipelines with state-approved corrosion control mechanisms by January 1, 1997. Smaller water suppliers were only required to replace their pipelines if lead and copper levels at the tap exceeded the action levels. To comply with the LCR, water suppliers were obligated to rigorously monitor water quality and implement improvements whenever necessary. This included ensuring that the water source itself was free of lead and copper and taking measures to reduce these metals in plumbing systems. Water treatment processes were adjusted to make the water as non-corrosive as possible. If suppliers failed to meet the LCR standards, they were required to adopt stricter filtration and monitoring methods. In some cases, replacing lead piping became necessary to maintain compliance. In January 2000, the EPA introduced the Lead and Copper Rule Minor Revisions (LCRMR), which required water suppliers to install the best available corrosion control mechanisms and continuously monitor water quality, even if corrosion control measures were already in place. These revisions became effective on April 11, 2000. The LCR faced criticism in 2003 when the Government Accountability Office (GAO) investigated the EPA following reports of elevated lead and copper levels in tap water in the District of Columbia. The GAO found that the EPA had not been collecting sufficient data on lead and copper levels from the states, despite claims that these levels had decreased. Data for 72% of water systems were missing. The lack of data was attributed to the EPA allocating more resources to lead regulation than to lead reporting.
